title: Write the alphabet
goal: Give the shapes a little time on paper.

study.title: Let your hand learn the shape.
paragraphs: Listening and singing can help you recognize the alphabet. Writing makes you look closely at where a line begins, which direction it moves, and how a letter is formed.
The aim is a clear, familiar shape. You do not need beautiful handwriting or speed. Use a pencil, an eraser, and lined paper; a guide sheet can help.

study.title: Watch. Trace. Try it yourself.
paragraphs: Watch how the letters are formed, then try them on paper. Trace a letter a few times, copy it, and finally write it without looking. Practice uppercase and lowercase forms.
items: Trace the shape a few times.
Write it from memory and compare.
Add a familiar word: A, a, apple.

study.title: Write names that mean something to you.
paragraphs: Begin with your own name. Names usually start with capital letters. Name order differs between languages and contexts; learn to recognize the forms you will use.
Next, write a few family members’ names and the names of three to five friends. Say each name and spell it letter by letter.
These are words you will use in introductions, reservations, forms, and accounts. Your letters are already doing something useful.

study.title: Keep it simple.
paragraphs: A pencil makes corrections easy. Lined paper or a beginner’s guide sheet helps you judge size and position. Typing and tapping do not replace this particular handwriting exercise.
Focus on ordinary print letters first. Cursive connects letters in a flowing style, but it is optional and can come later.
Do not rush toward a fixed deadline. Return for short sessions and aim for clear, recognizable forms.
